title: A blinded, prospective benchmark of in silico antibody discovery anchored to experimental affinity and developability - Nature Biotechnology
gist: AIntibody, a CASP-style blinded prospective benchmark, tested 511 AI-designed antibodies from 29 organizations against SARS-CoV-2 RBD across three tasks with uniform affinity and developability assays; AI could optimize antibodies in defined regimes (affinity maturation) and a few groups made developable sub-100 pM binders, but successes did not transfer across tasks, most models were worse than random clone picking at hit ranking, and a simple non-AI consensus method beat most AI designs.

themes.theme: Why a blinded prospective benchmark was needed

insights.claim: Experimentally validated prospective, blinded benchmarks are needed to separate durable advances from hype in computational antibody design, because most existing antibody-design benchmarks rely on retrospective analyses without additional experiments.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Investors evaluating AI-antibody startups should treat retrospective self-reported metrics as unreliable and demand blinded experimental validation.
insights.quote: Experimentally validated prospective, blinded benchmarks are needed to separate durable advances from hype in computational antibody design.

insights.claim: The challenge was deliberately primed for success by using the extensively characterized SARS-CoV-2 RBD target and providing sequencing datasets deeper and richer than typically available, so the results should be read as an upper bound on current computational capability, not general-purpose performance.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Real-world AI antibody performance on novel targets with sparse data is likely worse than these best-case numbers.
insights.quote: The results presented here should be interpreted as an upper bound on current computational capability for this target class, not as evidence of general-purpose performance across arbitrary antigens or data regimes.

insights.claim: AIntibody tested 511 AI-designed or predicted antibodies from 29 organizations across three tasks: in silico affinity maturation, affinity ranking within HCDR3 clusters, and out-of-library CDR design.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: A 29-organization field gives the first apples-to-apples read on who actually leads in AI antibody design.
insights.quote: AIntibody... tests 511 artificial intelligence (AI)-designed or predicted antibodies from 29 organizations on three tasks.

insights.claim: Participants spanned academic or nonprofit labs (10), AI biotechs (8), small or mid-size biotechs (5), large pharma (5) and big tech (1), with AI biotechs contributing the most sequences for the de novo design challenge.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Maps the competitive field and shows AI-native biotechs concentrate their bets on the hardest de novo design task.

themes.theme: Challenge 1: AI matches experimental affinity maturation

insights.claim: In the affinity maturation challenge, the top AI antibody reached 95 pM by KinExA, statistically indistinguishable from the best experimental antibody (113 pM), and the winning entry from Aureka represented a roughly 2,000-fold improvement over the parental antibody.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: AI can already match experimental affinity maturation when given deep sequencing data, potentially cutting 2-3 weeks from lead optimization.
insights.quote: The winning entry from Aureka achieved a 95 pM affinity, a 2,000-fold improvement over the parental antibody.

insights.claim: Aureka's model, if widely applicable and available, would reduce experimental time by 2-3 weeks by replacing an experimental combination library with a single in silico step, though eight of the participants could not design a single developable binder.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: The value of AI affinity maturation is real but concentrated in a few models; most tools still add no value.

insights.claim: ProBioGen's submission, an exact consensus-sequence match across all six CDRs derived with statistics and no machine learning, ranked third overall by KinExA at 540 pM with a perfect developability score.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: A simple statistical baseline beating most AI designs sets a sobering bar and questions the marginal value of complex models for in-library optimization.
insights.quote: statistical analysis of the selection data, without machine learning (ML), was sufficient to produce one of the top-performing designs in challenge 1.

themes.theme: Challenge 2: AI worse than random at hit ranking

insights.claim: Except for one model, AI prediction of high-affinity clones from clustered HCDR3 datasets was worse than random clone picking, with only 9.8-13.8% of AI submissions beating the cluster control versus 39% for randomly picked clones.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: For hit ranking, using AI was actively counterproductive versus a trivial baseline, a red flag for products marketed on this capability.
insights.quote: Except for one model, predicting high-affinity clones from clustered HCDR3 datasets was worse than random clone picking.

insights.claim: WashU was the only group to exceed the random baseline (50% versus 39%), yet even it was ineffective for cluster 27F and no winning algorithm transferred across all three clusters.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Even the single winner lacked cross-cluster generalization, underscoring that no model reliably ranks hits.

themes.theme: Challenge 3: high-variance de novo design and a scoring flaw

insights.claim: Out-of-library CDR design was highly variable, with many methods failing to outperform standard selections and 46.4% of submissions being nonbinders or nondevelopable binders.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: True de novo antibody design remains unreliable, so claims of general-purpose AI antibody generation should be discounted.
insights.quote: Out-of-library design was highly variable for most method submissions, with many failing to outperform standard selections.

insights.claim: Xencor's winning 2.9 pM out-of-library antibody failed to elute from the HIC column, a biophysical flaw that would probably be disqualifying under standard therapeutic development criteria, but won because the composite developability score let high affinity offset a single assay failure.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Headline affinity numbers can hide fatal developability flaws; future benchmarks will add go/no-go disqualification criteria.

themes.theme: Method classes and the case against one-model-for-everything

insights.claim: The best-performing method class varied by task: consensus or statistical methods won in-library affinity optimization, protein language model methods won out-of-library design, and no single class won cluster-level ranking.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Results argue for a portfolio of task-matched algorithms rather than one general model, shaping how to evaluate platform breadth claims.
insights.quote: These results argue against 'one model for everything' and point toward a portfolio approach where algorithms are applied opportunistically to specific tasks and available data.

insights.claim: Only one of the winners (Aureka) describes itself as an AI company; the others were academic groups (Scripps, UCSD, WashU) and medium-sized biotech Xencor, which won two challenges using two different algorithms without claiming AI expertise.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: The AI-antibody field remains open and deep pockets are not required to win, tempering the moat narrative around well-funded AI-native players.
insights.quote: It is striking that only one of the winners (Aureka) describes itself as an AI company.

insights.claim: Prediction of affinity changes will require orders of magnitude more highly diverse experimental data than presently available, and such discovery data are frequently siloed, encumbered by IP constraints and not machine readable.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: The binding constraint on AI antibody progress is proprietary, siloed experimental data, favoring players who can generate or aggregate it.
insights.quote: Prediction of affinity changes will require orders of magnitude of highly diverse experimental data, beyond those presently available.

insights.claim: Winning models were highly tuned to the specific data regimes provided and challenges 2 and 3 supplied extensive affinity data not representative of an early-stage discovery campaign, so it remains unproven whether these algorithms can transition from optimization to true discovery on data-sparse targets.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: The commercially valuable leap - AI discovery without deep affinity data - is still undemonstrated and is the focus of the 2026 challenge.
